claims.text: The starting protective coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure.
The starting coating has relatively diffuse or suboptimally distributed FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
Controlled annealing or post-deposition heat treatment can sharpen the FCC/BCC interfaces.
Thermal processing can refine and increase the density of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries can contribute to enhanced work hardening in a dual-phase high-entropy alloy.
Sharpened and refined FCC/BCC interphase boundaries are more effective obstacles to dislocation motion than the baseline boundaries.
Refined FCC/BCC interphase boundaries pin dislocations in the FCC matrix.
Interphase-boundary pinning increases the effective stress required for dislocation climb or glide.
Increasing the effective stress required for dislocation climb or glide reduces the creep strain rate.
Refining and increasing the density of FCC/BCC interfaces will enhance the coating's creep resistance under sustained loading.
Thermally processed coatings will have a lower secondary creep strain rate than the as-deposited baseline.
Thermally processed coatings will have a higher creep stress exponent than the as-deposited baseline.
Thermally processed coatings will show greater dislocation pile-up or pinning at FCC/BCC interfaces than the baseline.
The proposed mechanism operates under sustained loading at temperatures that preserve the dual-phase microstructure.
Temperatures below 800 degrees Celsius are within the phase-stable operating range of the unspecified coating.
Outside the phase-stable sustained-loading regime, other deformation mechanisms may govern creep.
The magnitude of the creep-resistance improvement and dislocation impediment is not yet quantitatively determined.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant creep-rate reduction or stress-exponent increase, or failure to observe enhanced interfacial dislocation obstruction, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
